finding.claim: update_doc calls can_edit() but discards the boolean result instead of calling require_edit(), so the authorization check is never enforced. Any caller with g.user set can overwrite the body of any document they neither own nor edit.
finding.source: Any user identified by g.user sending PUT /doc/<doc_id> with JSON {"body": ...} for a doc_id they have no rights to.
finding.sink: doc["body"] = request.json["body"] at docs.py:20 (modification of the document body).

trace.note: doc = DOCS[doc_id] fetched with no ownership check
can_edit(g.user, doc) returns False for non-editors, but the return value is ignored, so no abort(403)
By contrast, update_title correctly uses require_edit, which shows the intended control

finding.guards_checked: The only guard is the ignored can_edit() call. There is no before_request hook, decorator or other auth in the file. g.user is never set here, so it depends on external middleware (not present); even if that middleware authenticates the user, it does not authorize per document. The sibling endpoint update_title uses require_edit, confirming the check is missing here and not enforced elsewhere.

verdict.guard_found: can_edit() at docs.py:19 is a bare call whose boolean result is discarded; the aborting variant require_edit (docs.py:11-13) is used only in update_title (line 27). No decorator or before_request hook exists in the file.
verdict.reason: docs.py:19 calls can_edit(g.user, doc), which only returns a bool (docs.py:7-8) and is never tested, so docs.py:20 overwrites the body for any authenticated user, whereas update_title correctly calls require_edit at docs.py:27.
